title: Are we running out of sand?

turns.speaker: Nour
turns.text: Somebody told me sand is the second most extracted material on earth after water, and I assumed it was nonsense.

turns.speaker: Tavi
turns.text: It isn't. Concrete is mostly sand and gravel, and we pour an extraordinary amount of concrete.

turns.speaker: Ingrid
turns.text: The counterintuitive part is that desert sand is useless for it. Wind erosion makes the grains too round to lock together.

turns.speaker: Nour
turns.text: So countries surrounded by sand import it.

turns.speaker: Ingrid
turns.text: Routinely, yes. It's one of those facts that sounds invented.

turns.speaker: Tavi
turns.text: The extraction is where the damage is. River sand is dredged, and taking it out drops the riverbed, which takes the water table with it.

turns.speaker: Tavi
turns.text: Wells fail, bridges get undermined, and deltas stop being replenished so the coast erodes.

turns.speaker: Nour
turns.text: Is it actually scarce, though, or just badly managed?

turns.speaker: Ingrid
turns.text: Badly managed, mostly. It's abundant in absolute terms and locally exhausted, because it's heavy and not worth transporting far.

turns.speaker: Tavi
turns.text: Which is why illegal extraction is such a large business in some countries. The value is entirely in being nearby.

turns.speaker: Ingrid
turns.text: Crushed rock works and costs more. Recycled demolition concrete works for some uses and is barely used.

turns.speaker: Tavi
turns.text: Because the raw material is still cheap enough that nobody has to bother.

points: Sand is the second most extracted material after water, driven by concrete production.
Desert sand is unusable because wind-rounded grains do not interlock, so desert countries import sand.
River dredging lowers riverbeds and water tables, causing well failure, bridge undermining and coastal erosion through reduced delta replenishment.
Ingrid argues the problem is management rather than absolute scarcity, since sand is abundant but locally exhausted and uneconomic to transport.
Proximity value drives large-scale illegal extraction.
Crushed rock and recycled demolition concrete are viable substitutes but remain unused because raw sand is still cheap.
